#5189. Nanbeige4.3-33B Ties Qwen3.8-27B on Intelligence Index, but Spends 44% More Output Tokens

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K. Here is what that costs locally.

Two models just posted the same score. One needed 158,000 output tokens per task to get there. The other needed 110,000.

Nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5. According to Artificial Analysis's evaluation, published November 5, that matches Qwen3.8 27B at its xhigh reasoning setting. The model is open weights under Apache 2.0, accepts text only, and has a 524K-token context window.

Behind the tie sits a gap in effort. Artificial Analysis says Nanbeige used 158K output tokens per Intelligence Index task against 110K for Qwen3.8 27B, about 44% more. That weighted average covers answer and reasoning tokens across all nine v5 evaluations, including agentic tool-use turns. For anyone running these models, tokens translate into time, electricity or money, so the same score doesn't mean the same cost.

The Intelligence Index v5 combines nine evaluations, among them AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode 2.0 and AA-Omniscience. A score of 20 puts Nanbeige well above the 6 of Muse Glimmer, a 30B model in the same comparison. Artificial Analysis also notes that Nanbeige sets a new Pareto-optimal point for Intelligence Index against total parameters, since both it and Qwen3.8 27B are dense models. A larger mixture-of-experts model like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, by contrast, scores 33 while activating only 16B parameters per token.

The model card Nanbeige's lab published on Hugging Face describes the base model, positioned as the flagship teacher for the Nanbeige4.3 series. The lab says it will distill agentic capabilities into smaller models, such as an upcoming 3B version. On base-model benchmarks, the card shows 66.9 on MMLU-Pro against 59.3 for Gemma4-31B-Base. Those figures belong to the base model and are separate from the reasoning model's Intelligence Index result.

The two models reach 20 by different routes. Nanbeige scores 30% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 6% for Qwen, and 16% on the CritPt v2 Hard Subset against 4%. It also edges Qwen on AutomationBench-AA, 53% to 48%.

Elsewhere, it falls behind. On AA-Briefcase v1.1 it scores 1162 Elo against 1391, on FrontierCode 2.0 11% against 15%, and on HLE-Diamond 7% against 15%. The knowledge test tells the most distinctive story. On AA-Omniscience v1.1, Nanbeige scores -4 against Qwen's -6, with an 18% hallucination rate against 29%. Yet it answers only 29% of questions against 43%, declines 71% of them and gets 12% correct against 17%.

For general question answering, Qwen's higher accuracy is the better result.

Output tokens aren't a vanity metric. A reasoning model writes out its thinking as tokens, and every one costs decode time. If both models ran at the same speed on the same hardware, Nanbeige would take about 44% longer to finish a typical task.

Local decoding adds a second factor. Generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth, because each new token requires reading the model's weights, and a 33B dense model reads about 20% more weight data per token than a 27B dense model. Assuming the same quantization and the same memory-bound hardware, those two effects compound to roughly 1.7 times the wall-clock time per task. That figure is a back-of-the-envelope calculation, not a measured result.

Nor is there a hosted alternative to soften the blow. Artificial Analysis lists no confirmed public first-party or third-party APIs for Nanbeige, so unlike Qwen, which is sold per token through Alibaba's API, the cost is the hardware you run it on and the time it takes.

Artificial Analysis describes the model as small enough to run locally on a laptop, which holds true with a caveat. The weights are published in BF16, which at 33 billion parameters means roughly 66 GB, far beyond almost any laptop. At 8-bit, the weights fall to about 33 GB, and at 4-bit to about 17 GB, plus memory for the context cache. A machine with 24 GB of unified memory or more can plausibly hold a 4-bit build, though a long context will push it.

The vendor's own quickstart points the other way. The card's SGLang and vLLM examples both set tensor parallelism across four GPUs, which suggests the reference deployment is a multi-GPU server. Its Transformers example also enables trust_remote_code=True, which runs code from the repository. Reading that code first is the safer move, as is serving the model through vLLM or SGLang instead.

Quantization changes the model, too. The Intelligence Index numbers come from Artificial Analysis's own runs, so a 4-bit local build may score somewhat lower, or generate different token counts, than the version they evaluated.

This release is a clean example of why a headline score isn't enough. Nanbeige delivers Qwen-level results at 33B, with strengths in terminal tasks and physics reasoning and a more cautious answering style. The price for those strengths is length.

Anyone choosing between the two should run both on their own workload and record three numbers: the score on their tasks, output tokens per task and seconds per task on their hardware. For terminal-heavy, agentic work, Nanbeige's profile may justify the longer runs. For knowledge-heavy or latency-sensitive work, Qwen's shorter, more accurate answers look stronger.

Three signals are worth watching next: whether the 3B distilled version keeps the model's strengths, whether other labs report the same token behavior, and whether anyone publishes quantized local benchmarks. Until then, the simplest summary is also the most accurate: same score, different bill.

#5188. Ethereum maps post-AI, post-quantum cryptographic overhaul with Keccak-256 — Details

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Ethereum Foundation is in the news today after it announced that it has recommended Keccak-256 as the hash function for Ethereum’s hash-based cryptography.

The ongoing bear market price action is only a bump in the road. In the long term, however, the network has to be prepared to contend with threats posed by both quantum computing and progressing artificial intelligence capabilities.

On Tuesday, 24th November, the Foundation revealed its recommendation and the reasons behind it.

It considered five candidates: the ZK-friendly hashes, Poseidon and Poseidon2, the fast hashes BLAKE3 and BLAKE2, and the two hashes Ethereum already uses- SHA-256 and Keccak-256.

Keccak-256 has “arguably the most extensive cryptanalysis out of all unbroken traditional hashes,” the blog post read. An additional benefit is that this hash function has so far remained unaffected by AI-assisted cryptanalysis

Zero-knowledge proof technology improvements have removed the performance advantages offered by Poseidon. Security was the primary concern.

Though natively fast, the best collision attack reached 38 out of 64 rounds for SHA-256. Only 5 out of 24 rounds were reached for Keccak-256.

The Foundation also recommended against using SHA3-256 alongside Keccak-256 since both use the same underlying permutation and have similar security characteristics.

According to Ethereum Foundation Researcher Kev Wedderburn, they have been planning ways to counter quantum computing’s threat. In fact, AI has emerged as a more urgent risk recently.

Models are already finding bugs in production software faster than people can review them, the researcher wrote.

The planned upgrade will overhaul how validators sign messages, users authorize transactions, and how Ethereum verifies data posted by rollups.

It is harder than the 2022 Merge, and there is less time, Wedderburn acknowledged. Working faster can ship more bugs, so the Foundation has doubled the protocol security team to ensure formal verification. This will also allow the security work to progress at the pace of protocol development.

#5185. Five Forged Receipts Drained $304.5K From Ankr's Ethereum Bridge Using a 0.0044 ankrETH Deposit

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

SlowMist says five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit. Here is how the check failed.Every one of the five receipts was signed by the bridge's own trusted signer. Every one pointed to a deposit that had already been paid out.

On November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge. According to SlowMist's alert, the attacker built five forged receipts that all referenced a single legitimate Optimism transaction, changing the recipient, the token and the withdrawal amount in each one.

All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.

The reused transaction was tiny: a deposit of about 0.0044 ankrETH made on Optimism on November 3, which SlowMist's analysis says had already been redeemed on Ethereum the same day. Six days later, that one settled deposit was cited five times. The incident is recorded in the SlowMist Hacked database.Blockaid flagged the exploit as it unfolded, at about 08:42 UTC, with roughly $292,000 already gone. SlowMist followed at 09:14 UTC with the higher $304,500 estimate and an explanation of the forged receipts. Ankr paused withdrawals, and no recovery plan has been confirmed.

The design is common across lock-and-release bridges. A user deposits on the source chain, and an off-chain set of signers watches for that deposit and signs a receipt describing it. The destination contract, in this case Ankr's Ethereum bridge contract, checks that the receipt carries a valid signature and then releases the funds.That setup makes the signers the source of truth. The contract can't see Optimism, so it leans on the signature to prove the deposit happened. The weak point sits in the gap between "the signer signed this" and "this really happened." A contract that treats the first as proof of the second inherits every mistake the signing process makes.

SlowMist's finding is precise: the withdrawal function released assets without independently verifying the actual event on the source chain. A signature confirmed that the signer approved a message. It did not confirm that the message matched a deposit that existed, that was still unused, and that involved the same recipient, token and amount.The replay angle deserves attention, even though SlowMist's summary only implies it. A bridge normally marks each source event as consumed, keyed to something fixed like the source chain, transaction hash and log index, so it can be paid out once. If replay protection keys on the contents of the receipt instead, changing the recipient, token or amount produces a receipt the contract has never seen. Five edited receipts against one deposit would then look like five fresh claims. That is one plausible way the pieces fit together, not a finding the researchers have published.Bridge history offers parallels. In 2022, Wormhole lost about $325 million when an attacker got a forged message past its signature verification, and Nomad lost about $190 million after a misconfiguration let nearly any message pass as valid. The Ankr case is smaller, but it shares the same root: the verification step accepted something it shouldn't have.

The Ethereum transactions show the attacker extracted about 82.91 ankrETH, 515,206 ankrPOL and 7.98 million ANKR tokens. Blockaid described the five withdraw calls as using the tiny Optimism deposit to unlock the bridge's locked inventory and send it to a new wallet.The mix of assets tells its own story. Each forged receipt named a different token and amount, which suggests the attacker picked targets based on what the bridge held. That fits receipts built entirely by the attacker, apart from the one real transaction reference. Anyone wanting to trace them can open the bridge contract's transaction list on Etherscan and filter for the five `withdraw` calls on November 9.

The most important fact is still missing. SlowMist says the origin of the unauthorized signatures is under investigation, and it hasn't confirmed whether the signers were compromised.A valid signature on a forged receipt has a short list of explanations. A signing key, or the service holding it, could have been accessed. A signing service could have been tricked into signing attacker-supplied data. Or the signing logic itself could have a flaw that produces signatures for receipts it shouldn't. Each one points to a different fix: a stolen key means rotating signers, a manipulated service means tightening input validation off-chain, and a logic flaw means rewriting the signing rules.Whichever it turns out to be, the on-chain contract and the off-chain signer both failed to ask the same question. Either one verifying the source event would likely have stopped the attack, and neither did.

The lessons are narrow and practical. Replay protection should key on the immutable identity of the source event, not on the receipt's contents, and a source event should be consumable exactly once. The destination contract should confirm that the receipt's recipient, token and amount match what the source-chain event actually recorded, using a proof or an independent verifier instead of trusting the signer alone.Signer infrastructure needs its own scrutiny. Threshold schemes, hardware-backed keys and strict limits on what a signing service will sign all shrink the damage from a single failure. Rate limits and per-withdrawal caps help as well. A bridge that can release its entire locked inventory in five calls has no brake once a signature check is defeated.Trust in a bridge comes in layers, and one layer rarely holds up alone. Users with funds in Ankr's bridge should watch for the project's post-mortem and its plan for restoring withdrawals. For developers, the question to put to their own code is a blunt one: if a signer signs something false, what stops the contract from believing it?

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Bitcoin [BTC] witnessed yet another bout of volatility this week that caught the bulls off guard. On Wednesday, the 25th of November, Bitcoin bounced from a low of $57,300 to a local high of $61,622.

This bounce spurred the rest of the crypto market higher too, resulting in $406.85 million in long liquidations and $238.06 million in short liquidations.

The U.S. personal consumption expenditures (PCE) data was released on Wednesday. It rose 3.8% year-over-year, while core PCE rose 3.3% year-over-year.

Headline PCE in line with consensus estimates reinforced the market expectations of a 25-bps Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

A week ago, there was a 6.5% probability of a 50-point rate hike. At the time of writing, this probability was 0%.

It wasn’t bullish news, but it was a catalyst that allowed the price to jump higher and wipe out the dense cluster of short positions that had built up in recent days. Monday’s rally just past $64k was another short squeeze.

As things stand, demand is too weak and pessimism too intense for Bitcoin to mount an immediate comeback.

Founder and CEO of intelligence platform CryptoQuant, Ki Young Ju, noted that there was $16 billion in potential short liquidations from $60k to $100k, compared to just $5 billion in potential long liquidations.

In other words, a short squeeze was much more attractive in these conditions. Notably, a mini short squeeze occurred on Monday, as well as the recent price bounce back above $61k.

The Bitcoin active value to investor value ratio was back near 0.8 after climbing above 1.0 earlier this year, reported a crypto analyst. Moreno. It measures how far the spot price deviates from the True Market Mean, which is the aggregate on-chain cost basis for active investors.

Readings below 1 indicate active investors are carrying losses. Aggregate profitability has deteriorated since the BTC price rebound earlier this year.

The Bitcoin risk index was above 2 and neared its peak value from earlier this year. The metric shows higher readings during sell-offs, when capital turnover intensifies relative to market value.

The two metrics showed increasing stress on the market and offered a more attractive valuation to long-term buyers.

To make a compelling case for a bullish recovery, the selling pressure needs to be absorbed. The evidence at hand does not support sizeable demand- for example, Bitcoin spot ETF flows have been overwhelmingly bearish in November.

#5182. How Bittensor's Gamma Turns Every AI Payment Into an Alpha Burn

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Paying a Bittensor subnet with gamma burns its alpha token. Here is how gamma gets minted, how the lower-price rule works and why the credit can never be converted back.Pay a Bittensor subnet for an AI answer with gamma, and your payment vanishes. The alpha token behind it gets burned, the credit gets spent, and nobody can redeem either one.

Using a subnet's service today usually means creating an account, adding funds and collecting an API key, and every additional subnet repeats the routine. Opentensor announced gamma to cut that friction. With gamma, a Bittensor wallet handles both access and payment across any subnet that adopts the standard.The mechanics are laid out in the gamma guide in the subtensor docs. Gamma is a credit a subnet can accept as payment, valued in US dollars. A customer gets it by burning that subnet's alpha token, and each dollar of burned alpha value mints one gamma, so a burn valued at $100 creates 100 gamma.Each balance stays tied to the subnet where it was created. Gamma minted for subnet 51 can't pay for a service on any other subnet. Root switches the system on network-wide, and each subnet owner or lease beneficiary then enables it for their own subnet.

Customers have two ways in. They can pay with TAO, and the protocol buys the subnet’s alpha and burns it in a single transaction. Or they can pay with alpha they already hold on that subnet, and the protocol burns it directly to create gamma.

Setup takes four steps. The customer creates a fresh hotkey that will act as an API key, associates it with their coldkey, looks up the service they want and mints. The docs give the command: btcli gamma mint --netuid 51 --hotkey API_KEY --amount-tao 10 --service-hotkey SERVICE_HOTKEY. The TAO route follows the same pool and flow accounting as stake-burn and creates no stake position. Users who hold stake can burn it with mint-gamma-with-stake, and --amount-alpha all burns the whole position.

The gamma lands in a deposit. Each deposit belongs to the minting coldkey and is keyed by the API-key hotkey, which signs the customer's requests. A hotkey holds at most one deposit per subnet, and a coldkey holds at most 64 per subnet. The docs warn against reusing a staking hotkey or a coldkey, because requests signed with the key get paid from the deposit.A few guardrails apply. A mint must reach at least 0.1 gamma. By default, the SDK quotes the mint first and fails it if the result lands more than 5% below the quote. The mint also needs a TAO/USD price no older than 300 blocks, about an hour.

Gamma’s valuation rule decides how much credit a burn buys. The protocol values the burned alpha in TAO, then converts that figure to dollars through an on-chain TAO/USD price feed. The TAO value equals alpha multiplied by the lower of two prices, the gamma price and the spot price, which the docs write as alpha × min(gamma price, spot price).

Every subnet keeps a gamma price. When a subnet registers, the price starts at the median alpha price across subnets. After that it moves asymmetrically. If spot falls, the gamma price falls to match at once. If spot rises, the gamma price climbs slowly toward it, closing a small slice of the gap each block, so the gap halves every 600 blocks, roughly two hours. However high spot jumps, the gamma price can at most double every 600 blocks.An example shows the effect. Say a user burns 100 alpha when spot sits at 0.05 TAO but the gamma price lags at 0.04. The mint uses 0.04, which gives 4 TAO of value, and at $400 per TAO that mints 1,600 gamma. Had the gamma price caught up, the same burn would mint 2,000, so the lag costs the burner 400 gamma. A short-lived pump buys no extra credit. The figures are illustrative, but the rule comes straight from the docs.The TAO/USD feed gets similar damping. A root-controlled oracle supplies the price, and the accepted price falls to a lower feed immediately but rises at most 66 parts per million per block, about 2% an hour. The docs admit the oracle is trusted: its accepted price can climb up to roughly 61% a day until root replaces or removes it.One more detail matters. The docs say alpha is valued at these prices, not at what selling it would return, so a burn that is large relative to the pool is worth more than a sale would be. A big burner gets credit for full value instead of a slipped sale price.Once minted, gamma holds its dollar value whether TAO or alpha prices rise or fall. Service providers still set their own prices.

To use a service, a person or an AI agent signs a request with a hotkey from their Bittensor wallet. The subnet owner, or another authorized account, deducts the required credits from that hotkey's gamma balance before delivering the service. Nothing transfers to anyone. The designated spender calls `spend-gamma` with up to 512 entries per call, each naming a hotkey, an amount and a 32-byte reference, and the spent gamma is destroyed on the spot.The reference doubles as a receipt. By convention it holds the service's own ID for the request being paid, returned with the response, so the customer can match each spend to a specific request. The chain repeats the reference in its events and reads it nowhere else, so an entry sent twice spends twice.Customers keep control throughout. The minting coldkey can set a daily spend cap that refills linearly over 7,200 blocks, about a day, and a cap of zero pauses the deposit. The coldkey can also change the spender, keep separate deposits for different apps and agents, and top up an existing deposit without switching hotkeys. Because the coldkey can pause or redirect at any moment, services spend ahead: they spend what they are about to serve, then serve what was spent. A spender can hand this right to a `GammaSpend` proxy, which can make no other call.Both minting and spending leave public records on-chain, so anyone can audit how much credit a subnet has created and how much customers have used.

The limits are strict. Gamma can't be transferred to another wallet, and it can't be converted back into alpha or TAO. It confers no claim on any party and can't be redeemed. Each subnet chooses whether, and at what prices, it accepts its own gamma.

The docs flag the sharpest risk directly: dissolving or pruning a subnet destroys all of its gamma, and holders receive nothing. A customer who prepaid a large deposit to a subnet that later shuts down loses it. Moving gamma between your own deposits is allowed, and a deposit opened under someone else's hotkey stays yours, since you can pull the gamma back at any time.A coldkey swap adds a few wrinkles. While one is announced, the coldkey's gamma calls are refused, though its spenders keep spending. After a subnet owner swaps coldkeys, deposits that name the old one keep it until the owner republishes its service.

The docs answer the economic question in one sentence: spent gamma pays its spender nothing. The value of the burned alpha accrues to the subnet's alpha holders.

That makes gamma a direct demand mechanism for alpha. Creating gamma always burns the subnet's alpha, which removes those tokens from circulation for good. When customers pay with TAO, the protocol first buys alpha from the subnet's pool, so TAO-funded purchases add buying pressure before the burn. Every dollar of AI usage ties a purchase of service credits to a burn of alpha.

A service operator earns through the alpha it holds and the emissions its subnet receives, not through a payment from customers. The structure rewards subnets that attract real usage, since usage shrinks their alpha supply.Two questions remain open. Customers get dollar-denominated credit, but the burn that funds it follows alpha prices, so heavy usage during a price spike may feel expensive. Holders also carry the dissolution risk, which will push careful buyers toward established subnets. Which services accept gamma, and at what price, will show whether this becomes a real payments layer or a niche tool. The mechanism is clear, and adoption is the unknown.

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Zcash holders just got a new update as the major crypto exchange Gemini has announced support for Shielded Zcash deposits.

Scott Merkel, 'Wolf of All Streets,' shared this update in an X post, highlighting the milestone as the first of its kind for any major exchange. According to Merkel, Gemini now lets customers deposit Zcash (ZEC) to shielded addresses, saying it is the first major exchange with both shielded deposits and withdrawals.

GEMINI NOW LETS CUSTOMERS DEPOSIT ZCASH $ZEC TO SHIELDED ADDRESSES, SAYING IT IS THE FIRST MAJOR EXCHANGE WITH BOTH SHIELDED DEPOSITS AND WITHDRAWALS https://t.co/d9pIFJ6uJM

Gemini co-founder Tyler Winklevoss shared the milestone in a recent X post, adding that the recent move builds on the launch of shielded Zcash withdrawals on Gemini this summer.

In July 2026, shortly after the Ironwood upgrade was activated, Gemini launched support for shielded Zcash withdrawals to the new Ironwood pool, allowing users to send Zcash from Gemini to their Ironwood deposit address. Ironwood (NU6.3) went live on July 28, 2026, at block height 3,428,143, bringing a new shielded pool for Zcash.

With the recent launch of support for Shielded Zcash deposits, Gemini users can make Shielded Zcash deposits and withdrawals to and from Ironwood, with Winklevoss remarking that the private movement of money was now complete.

Zcash's total shielded supply now sits at around 4.93 million ZEC (around 28.94% of total ZEC supply) as of November 25, 2026.

November has brought in key updates for the Zcash network. Zcash's NU7 upgrade went live earlier in November 2026, slashing ZEC's target block time to 25 seconds from 75 seconds. The new 25-second block target lets miners add a batch of transactions to the chain three times as often.

None of this prints extra ZEC. Each block pays a third as much and halvings come every 5,040,000 blocks instead of 1,680,000, so the issuance schedule holds at roughly four years per halving.

Days after the NU7 upgrade, the Zcash Foundation followed up with the release of Zebra 7.1.0, which fixed ten security advisories, most of which closed off ways in which another node on the network (a peer) could stop a Zebra node from catching up with the chain or make it run out of memory. It also added sync and memory diagnostics, automatic peer recovery, and clearer errors.

#5180. Enjin Matrixchain Votes on OpenGov Today: What Changes for ENJ Holders on November 16

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Enjin holders vote through November 13 on moving Matrixchain to OpenGov on November 16. Here is how the nine tracks, the 1,000 ENJ deposit and conviction voting work, and what the Relaychain vote shows.

Enjin's new proposal deposit sounds steep at 1,000 ENJ. It's actually the cheap part.

Enjin holders have until today, November 13, to vote on moving the Matrixchain to the Fort Canning release. The referendum opened November 10. If it passes, the upgrade is targeted for November 16 at block #12,319,600, with the network moving from runtime 1.3.1 to 1.4.3. Enjin's Fort Canning announcement lays out the plan, and the official changelog carries the technical detail.

The Relaychain has already made the jump. Referendum #16 approved its upgrade on October 28, and it went live on November 9. The Matrixchain vote is the second half of one upgrade, and it is the half that changes how Matrixchain makes decisions from then on.

Early coverage reported the schedule and the headline numbers: nine tracks, 1,000 ENJ. The changelog and the governance portal show the mechanics behind them, and those mechanics change more than the headlines suggest.

Today, the Matrixchain runs its governance through the older Democracy, Council and Technical Committee pallets, the modules that handle proposals and votes. Fort Canning replaces all three with a new set: Referenda, Conviction Voting, Origins, Whitelist and the Enjin Fellowship. Under OpenGov, any account can submit a referendum on one of nine tracks, and from the moment the upgrade lands, Matrixchain's own upgrades go through that process.

A track is a lane for a particular kind of decision. Enjin's changelog describes the families: Root and the admin tracks for the highest-stakes changes, Whitelisted Caller for proposals the Fellowship fast-tracks, and two special tracks, Referendum Killer and Referendum Canceller, for stopping a proposal that shouldn't proceed. Matrixchain gets no treasury tracks: those, sized by how much a proposal would spend, stay on the Relaychain, where treasury requests now go. Each track has its own deposit, approval curve and enactment period, and the Enjin Fellowship can fast-track time-sensitive proposals.

Splitting decisions this way means a small treasury request doesn't face the same bar as a change to the chain's core. Riskier tracks demand larger deposits and more support, while smaller ones move faster and cost less.

The submission deposit rises from 0.025 ENJ to 1,000 ENJ on every track, a 40,000-fold increase. The deposit is refunded when a referendum passes or is canceled, and it exists to deter spam. As an illustration, using the roughly $66 million market cap reported in early October, ENJ traded near three cents, which would put 1,000 ENJ around $33.

That is only the entry ticket. The cost that matters comes next. A referendum also needs a decision deposit before it moves into voting, and the changelog lists steep figures: 2,500,000 ENJ on Root and Fellowship Admin, 1,000,000 ENJ on the other admin tracks, and 2,500 to 250,000 ENJ on the Relaychain's treasury tracks. At the same illustrative price, the 2.5 million ENJ Root deposit comes to roughly $80,000, about 0.12% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance.

So proposing is cheap, and pushing a proposal through is not. Anyone can raise an idea, but anyone who wants the network to vote on something big needs real stake in the outcome. The changelog says the same values apply on both chains, and Matrixchain adopts them for its new tracks.

The best evidence of how these votes work comes from the Relaychain referendum that has already finished. Enjin's governance portal shows referendum #16 as finalised, approved on October 28 and enacted on November 9.

The final tally on the page is small. Eleven voters cast 381,303.02 ENJ of conviction-weighted voting power, and all of it went to Aye: 100% in favor, 0 ENJ against. The page also shows raw, unweighted support of 271,303.2 ENJ, which it describes as the total balance backing the proposal and the figure the support curve uses. The conviction multiplier on the page runs from under 1x up to 6x.

Two numbers stand out. First, an entire chain upgrade passed with 271,303 ENJ of raw support, about 0.013% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance, a figure worked out from the portal's number. Second, conviction added about 110,000 ENJ of weight on top of the raw balance, an average multiplier of roughly 1.4x. Voters picked up some extra weight, but most didn't lock their tokens for the long periods that earn the top multipliers.

A 100% Aye result says little by itself. A scheduled upgrade with no organized opposition passes easily, and the tally shows how thin engagement was.

Fort Canning adds the safeguard that thin turnout calls for. A referendum now needs a minimum share of total ENJ voting in support. The changelog sets 0.5% on Root and the admin tracks, 0.005% to 0.125% on the Relaychain's treasury tracks, 0.1% for Referendum Killer and 0.05% for Referendum Canceller. Measured against 2.02 billion ENJ, that means about 10.1 million ENJ on Root, roughly 101,000 to 2.5 million on the treasury tracks, about 2.02 million to kill a referendum and about 1.01 million to cancel one.

Referendum #16's 271,303 ENJ of raw support would clear the lowest treasury floor of about 101,000 ENJ, but it would miss the Root floor by a factor of about 37. The page doesn't show which track the referendum used, and a runtime upgrade typically sits on a high-stakes track, so the Root comparison works as an illustration and not as a finding. The floors also didn't exist when #16 passed, since Fort Canning introduced them.

That is the real change. Under the new rules, 11 wallets can't carry a chain-level decision on their own. Low turnout means failure, and proposals that matter will need far more ENJ behind them. Enjin's changelog says Matrixchain upgrades go through OpenGov starting with this one, which suggests today's vote still runs on the current system, so the floors will first bite on the first OpenGov referendum.

Holders who haven't voted can still do so through Enjin's governance portal before the window closes. Voting locks tokens, so the lock length is worth checking first. Enjin's support article on voting explains the trade-off: the longer the lock, the more a vote counts, and tokens stay locked until the period ends.

Node operators on the Matrixchain can wait for the result before upgrading, as Enjin has indicated, and then follow the changelog for the version to install. Relaychain operators already needed client version 1.8.1.

This vote is more about control than speed. OpenGov spreads decisions across tracks with deposits and support floors built for the weight of each choice, and it moves ENJ holders from voting on a handful of items to a standing governance system. The Relaychain's first vote showed how little participation it took under the old rules, and the first referenda after November 16 will show whether holders turn out for the new ones. If most proposals stall at the decision deposit, the system costs too much. If they clear with a handful of voters, the floors aren't doing their job. Either result will tell holders what their ENJ can do.

#5178. BlackRock ETF Dumps 1 Million ETH Worth $1.75B as Ethereum Outflows Accelerate: Is ETH In Trouble?

BlackRock’s Ethereum ETF has lost over 1 million ETH worth $1.75 billion since October as outflows accelerate.

The BlackRock ETF has shed more than 1 million ETH since October 1, recording net outflows of 1,018,839 ETH worth approximately $1.75 billion. The selling continued on Monday, as BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust (ETHA) transferred another batch of coins to Coinbase Prime.

Between 11:52 and 12:02 UTC, four separate transfers moved 42,631 ETH from BlackRock’s deposit addresses to Coinbase Prime, the brokerage desk handling the fund’s trades. The transfers were worth approximately $73 million at Monday’s prices.

Since October 1, #BlackRock has seen net outflows of 1,018,839 $ETH ($1.75B).https://t.co/YfaFJXVOID pic.twitter.com/tfljcmoSsM

— Lookonchain (@lookonchain) November 23, 2026

The outflows have taken a large bite out of the fund. Comparing Lookonchain’s data with BlackRock’s own filings confirms the match to the coin. ETHA now holds less Ethereum than it did at the end of June.

How much has the BlackRock ETF lost so far, and what might this mean for ETH?

ETHA held 3,675,697 ETH on September 30, its quarterly report shows. On November 20, the iShares fund page listed 2,656,857 ETH.

That is a drop of 1,018,840 ETH, or 28%, which lines up with Lookonchain’s count almost exactly. Shares outstanding fell by a similar amount, from 162.4 million to 119.1 million, as investors cashed out.

The timing stings. In the third quarter, the BlackRock ETF bought 1.19 million ETH for $2.71 billion as money poured back in. Nearly all of that has now left. ETHA’s 2,656,857 ETH is below the 2,695,456 it held on June 30.

The fund’s net assets stood at $4.31 billion on November 20. Its net asset value per share has fallen 41% this year.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Predicts Best Low-Cap Crypto

We traced the Arkham-labelled addresses in Lookonchain’s screenshot on the Ethereum blockchain. Two BlackRock deposit addresses, 0xC8c5…5b95 and 0x01c2…59E5, sent every transfer to two Coinbase Prime hot wallets.

Since October 1, the two addresses made 84 transfers totalling 1,128,667 ETH. Priced at the hour each one moved, that is about $2.54 billion, or an average of $2,254 per ETH.

The pace picked up in November. The weeks starting November 2 and November 9 each saw more than 200,000 ETH leave, compared with 120,000 to 170,000 a week in October. The biggest single days were October 7, November 10 and November 20, at more than 70,000 ETH each.

The on-chain total is higher than the net drop in holdings because some new money still came in. It also includes Monday’s transfers, which are not yet in the fund’s November 20 figures.

These moves do not mean BlackRock is selling for itself. Coinbase acts as the trust’s agent, and ETHA pays out redemptions either in ETH or in cash raised by selling ETH. When investors leave the fund, the coins go out through Coinbase Prime.

EXPLORE: BitMine’s Estimated $3.6B ETH Loss Overshadows Stock Edge

ETH trades at $1,724, below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $2,131, and its 200-day EMA at $2,248. It fell to $1,538 on November 21, just above its June low of $1,506.

Monday’s 42,631 ETH shows the BlackRock ETF redemptions have not stopped. A pause in transfers to Coinbase Prime would be the first sign the selling is easing.

Crypto has an AI sector of its own, and from the outside it looks like one trade. Up close, the projects in it do very different jobs, and a comparison only makes sense once you know which job each one does.

Part of the sector already earns real revenue. Venice, a private AI app, became a unicorn in July 2026 with a $65 million Series A, and its CEO, Erik Voorhees, told TechCrunch that the company is profitable, with annualized run-rate revenues of over $70 million. People pay for private AI.

The map goes layer by layer, and each project is described from its own site.

The base layer connects idle graphics cards with the people who need them.

Most of what this layer sells is time on hardware, though Akash and io.net now also sell access to open models through APIs. For teams weighing a rented GPU against their own hardware, Lightchain AI has published a comparison of self-hosting an LLM and a worker network.

Here the network itself decides whose work is best, and pays for it.

This layer competes with ChatGPT on the user’s side of the screen.

Lightchain is building an agents layer of its own, Lightchain Agents, with a waitlist open now.

This is where Lightchain AI sits. It is a layer-1 blockchain built to run AI. Its blog keeps a plain list of what is live on the network today.

Lightchain also touches three of the other layers:

The sector will keep trading as one theme. It works more like a stack, where each layer needs the others: GPUs to run on, models worth running, apps people want, agents that act, and a record that shows what happened. Lightchain’s bet is on that last layer: the more AI runs on open networks, and the more agents pay one another, the more a public record of who served each answer matters.

Lightchain AI is a layer-1 blockchain for AI. Independent operators stake LCAI and serve open models such as gpt-oss, Qwen3, and Llama from their own GPUs. The chain assigns each job, holds the fee in escrow, and keeps a record of every job that anyone can look up. Products live today include Lightchain Chat, Lightchain Desktop (beta), Lightchain Studio, the Lightchain Bridge, and the Lightscan explorer. The LCAI DUNA, a Wyoming association, is the project’s legal entity.

Website: lightchain.ai · X: @LightchainAI · Discord: discord.gg/lightchain

This has drawn attention across the crypto market as the price of XRP suffered larger losses this month compared with last month, sparking questions about whether investor confidence is recovering.

#5174. NEAR’s Inflation Cut: The Math Behind a 5.27% to 3.37% Staking Yield

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

HSP-029 lowers NEAR’s issuance cap from 2.5% to 1.6% over 24 months. The cap formula, the epoch step and the yield math show what that does to stakers.

Most headlines on NEAR’s new inflation schedule stop at “2.5% to 1.6%.” Stakers feel a different number. They earn about 5.27% today and will earn roughly 3.37% once the cut finishes, and a single line of arithmetic accounts for the gap.

House of Stake ratified HSP-029 on November 16, after the Security Council’s 14-day veto window passed without a veto. The proposal touches one parameter, the maximum annual issuance rate, which drops from 2.5% to 1.6% over 24 months. It is the second cut in just over a year, coming after the October 2025 halving from 5%.

Everything else stays put. Issuance still splits 90% to staking participants and 10% to the protocol treasury. There is no new spending program, no validator subsidy and no automatic trigger that could push issuance back up. The full proposal models 11.8 million NEAR of issuance avoided over two years and 66.1 million over six, measured against leaving the cap at 2.5%.

The schedule is a straight line with no stair steps:

Here t is the number of months since the reduction begins. The 0.9% is the total drop (2.5 minus 1.6), and dividing it by 24 gives a monthly step of 0.0375 percentage points, or 3.75 basis points. The min(t, 24) term caps the ramp at month 24, and the cap sits at 1.6% from there on.

NEAR applies the step every epoch rather than once a month. An epoch lasts about 12 hours, so the cap slips by roughly 0.0006 percentage points each time, far too little to notice on any given day. There are no step dates to mark on a calendar. Sampled every six months, the line looks like this:

The yield column uses the math in the next section. It drops about 0.08 percentage points a month, evenly, with no cliff.

New tokens go mostly to stakers, so the staked pool splits the reward, and a smaller pool earns more per token. That gives a working formula:

gross yield ≈ 0.9 × issuance cap ÷ staking ratio

The 0.9 is the staker share of issuance. Using the proposal’s figures, 0.9 × 2.5% ÷ 0.4271 comes to 5.27%, where 42.71% is the staking ratio reported when the proposal went to vote. Put in the 1.6% cap and 0.9 × 1.6% ÷ 0.4271 gives 3.37%, the same number the proposal publishes. Anyone can check the headline yields on a calculator.

The formula has two limits. It uses the cap, but realized issuance runs a little lower because transaction fees are burned. HSP-029 measured 2.45% in September, which puts today’s yield near 5.16%. The staking ratio also moves. When more people stake, the same rewards spread over more tokens and yield falls further, and when people unstake it climbs. The 3.37% figure assumes today’s ratio holds.

Stakers feel it first. By the proposal’s own math, someone staking 1,000 NEAR ends up with about 20 fewer tokens after two years than if the cap had stayed at 2.5%. The numbers back that up: yield averages about 4.32% across the ramp, roughly 0.95 points under today’s rate for two years.

Holders who don’t stake come out ahead. More than half of NEAR’s supply sits unstaked, and every new token dilutes those holdings. Trimming the cap by 0.9 percentage points trims that dilution by the same amount each year. Stakers give up some reward so that everyone else gives up less value.

Validators get an easier path than in 2025, when the halving cut staking rewards from about 9% to 4.75% in a single upgrade. Operators now have 24 months to plan. NEAR’s analysis finds that most validator revenue comes from commission on delegated stake, so service quality and fee competition shape income more than the issuance rate does.

Recent history explains the setup. When the 2025 halving shipped, an earlier community poll had missed the two-thirds threshold, and critics said the core team pushed the change through anyway. HSP-029 sidesteps that argument by design.

Two separate approvals are required. Token holders voting through veNEAR set the direction, and that vote closed November 2 with 99.96% in favor and none against. Validators then decide on their own whether to adopt the protocol upgrade that makes the cap binding. The author, Sal Ternullo of SVRN, opened discussion on October 7, and the process ran through the Screening Committee and Security Council in public. Raising issuance again would take a new proposal and another round of validator adoption, so nothing can be added quietly later.

Ratification does not change issuance yet. A one-quarter grace period comes first, giving wallets, exchanges, custodians and staking providers time to update their disclosures. NEAR One then releases the upgrade and validators choose whether to adopt it, with the reduction starting about a quarter after ratification. On schedule, that means a start in early 2027 and a 1.6% cap around early 2029.

Three things are worth tracking. Validator adoption of the upgrade comes first, because the cap stays at 2.5% until enough validators run it. The staking ratio comes next, since it moves yield regardless of the formula. Last are the quarterly transparency reports NEAR has promised, which compare realized issuance with the schedule.

Price is a separate question. Lower issuance eases supply pressure, but nothing in it creates demand. The cap will follow its published line down, and yield will follow the cap.

BTC gave back its Nvidia pump in six hours. ETFs keep selling, and Strategy spent $4.30 on STRC per $1 on bitcoin.

Bitcoin was supposed to catch a break. Instead, based on today’s Bitcoin news, November 24, BTC trades near $60,400, below where it stood before Nvidia brought back Jensen Huang. Monday’s excitement barely lasted six hours before the market gave it all back.

Nvidia held on to its gains, closing Monday at $165.05, up 31%. Bitcoin wasn’t so lucky. BTC briefly climbed 5.7% after the announcement, only to slide below its pre-news price by mid-afternoon in New York. By early Tuesday, it had fallen below $61,000 again. Another rally, another disappointment.

The jump that followed Monday’s announcement was gone within six hours.

The selling in this week’s Bitcoin news has company. US spot Bitcoin ETFs posted a fifth straight day of outflows on Monday, and Strategy, the biggest corporate buyer, added just 457 BTC last week.

Strategy has acquired 457 $BTC and repurchased $212M of $STRC. We increased our Digital Credit Securities Repurchase Program by $1B and reallocated $1B from our USD Reserve to USD Cash. As of 11/22/26, we hold 851,305 BTC and $4.8B of USD Assets. $MSTR https://t.co/Wklom6dzrm

— Michael Saylor (@saylor) November 23, 2026

So is Bitcoin’s bounce from $55,000 a real turn, and how much buying is Michael Saylor’s company actually doing?

If you thought you missed yesterday’s reversal and regretted not FOMOing into the pump, you’re probably glad you didn’t. Bitcoin not only gave back the entire pump but also retraced below its initial price before the pump. Absolute cinema.

We tracked Binance’s minute-by-minute BTC price around the Nvidia news.

The contrast with Nvidia is the story. The chipmaker’s rally was about its own leadership, and it held. Bitcoin’s was borrowed, and once traders took profits, nothing was there to keep it up.

That leaves BTC stuck near $60,000, about 10% above Saturday’s two-year low of $55,130 but below the levels it lost last week.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Predicts Best New Crypto to Hodl

The fund flows behind the Bitcoin news have not turned. US spot Bitcoin ETFs lost a net $569.7 million on Monday, November 23, figures from SoSoValue’s ETF dashboard show. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $509.3 million of it.

It was the fifth straight day of outflows. The week before, the funds lost $1.79 billion, the third-largest weekly outflow since they launched in January 2024. Total net assets have dropped to about $74.1 billion.

That is a lot of selling for one buyer to absorb, even the biggest one.

EXPLORE: Bitcoin Below $62K After Anthropic IPO: Is a SpaceX Style Crash Coming?

Saylor has spent the sell-off signalling that Strategy will keep buying. “The dots aren’t done,” he posted on Sunday, November 22, alongside the company’s purchase tracker.

The filings tell a more cautious story. Strategy bought 457 BTC for $29.6 million in the week to November 22, at an average of $64,898, its latest SEC filing shows. It now holds 851,305 BTC at an average cost of $75,446.

For this Bitcoin news story, we added up Strategy’s three November filings to see where the money went. Strategy raised $705 million by selling MSTR shares over those three weeks. Only $145 million went into bitcoin.

Most of the rest went to buying back STRC, Strategy’s high-yield preferred stock, which has been trading below its face value. Strategy spent $628 million on those repurchases, $4.30 for every $1 it put into bitcoin. Last week, bitcoin took just 12% of the total.

The buying has also slowed fast. Strategy added 1,036 BTC in the first week of November, 485 in the second and 457 in the third. Last week’s $29.6 million equals less than 2% of what the ETFs sold in the week before.

Strategy still has firepower. It raised its buyback limit for preferred stock from $3 billion to $4 billion this week, and it holds $4.8 billion in cash. But MSTR, at $84.40 on Monday, is valued at only about 1.0 times its bitcoin once debt and preferred stock are counted, our estimate shows. At that level, selling new shares no longer adds bitcoin per share, which helps explain why Saylor’s dots keep getting smaller.

BTC trades at $60,448, below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $72,510, and its 200-day EMA at $74,867.

For this Bitcoin news cycle to turn, the ETF selling has to stop first. Until it does, Strategy’s weekly few hundred coins will not be enough to lift BTC above $62,300.

#5172. French Senate Rejects Disclosure Rule for Crypto

French senators on Nov. 24 rejected a proposal that would have required taxpayers to disclose self-hosted cryptocurrency holdings exceeding €100,000.

They would have had to report those assets as of Dec. 31.

This would have been the case even if they had held the same coins since January without making any sales.

Two matching amendments to the French 2027 budget were rejected by the Senate during the first reading of the draft.

Senators Pascal Savoldelli and Anne-Sophie Romagny reintroduced the proposal after it briefly passed in the National Assembly earlier in the month.

French taxpayers must disclose their crypto assets held on foreign crypto platforms.

These amendments would have expanded disclosure requirements to wallets that owners directly control. This pertains to a wallet that is not managed by an exchange or another custodian.

The French National Assembly approved the €100,000 disclosure threshold in a 150-44 vote on Nov. 3. There were also eight abstentions.

The next day, the National Assembly voted down the entire revenue portion of the budget.

This vote brought down the wallet disclosure provision along with the rest of the budget.

However, the subsequent effort to revive the provision in the Senate was defeated.

It should be noted that the 2027 budget is still being considered at the time of writing.

The Senate also rejected two other crypto-related measures debated as part of the budget.

One was a provision to tax gains realized when holders exchange cryptocurrencies for certain stablecoins.

The second was a proposal to expand France's exit tax to include unrealized gains on cryptocurrencies held by taxpayers who move their tax residence outside the country.

#5170. Why Does AI Get Simple Questions Wrong? What Google's Humanity's First Exam Shows

You ask an AI model to name the color of the third letter in each word on a neon sign. It gets it right. You ask again, and it slips by one letter. Nothing broke.

The model could do the task. It just did not do it every time. Google DeepMind built a test for exactly that gap, and the results show how far "usually right" can sit from "reliably right."

Most AI benchmarks ask a model to solve a hard problem once. If it passes, it scores. Google DeepMind's Humanity's First Exam (HFE), released on November 24, 2026, asks something different. Can a model solve an easy task, and slight rewrites of it, every single time?

The prompts are elementary on purpose. They cover counting objects, naming colors, tracking where something moved, basic arithmetic, strict formatting rules and spotting false premises. Humans solve them in about a minute.

One public example: "List the color of the third letter of each word in the neon sign in order, separated by a semicolon." The answer is green; yellow; white; blue; blue.

The paper calls the difference the Family Reliability Gap. One slip anywhere in the 16 answers fails the whole family.

The top five models score 96% to 98% on a single try and 100% on family pass@4. Their family pass⁴ averages only 85.8%. Across all 18 models, the gap runs from 7.6 to 80.1 percentage points.

The bottom row is the sharpest case. That model gets 68.7% of single tries right, yet clears only 18.6% of question families every time. Its family pass@4 is 98.8%, so it could solve nearly every family at least once.

The math is simple. Say a model is right 90% of the time on each answer, and the answers are independent. Getting 16 in a row right happens about 18.5% of the time (0.9 to the 16th power). That is a rough illustration, not the paper's calculation, but it shows how small error rates compound.

The paper's own example makes the same point. One model trails the leader by 6.6 points on single tries and by 29.4 points on family pass⁴. On average, about half the shortfall comes from prompts a model always fails. The other half comes from flakiness: right on some runs, wrong on others.

Humans and models also struggle in opposite places. People were least accurate on math and logic seeds. Models were strongest there and weakest on counting and reading text inside images.

Traders now hand AI tools real jobs: reading a contract, summarizing a token page, checking a wallet address in a screenshot, or running a bot. In those jobs, one wrong character or one miscounted number is the whole failure. A model that is right 19 times out of 20 will still be wrong on the 20th, and a signed transaction cannot be undone.

1. Ask twice. Run the same question more than once. If the answers differ, treat both as unconfirmed.

2. Check the visual parts yourself. Counts, colors, positions and text read from an image are where models slip most. Compare addresses and numbers character by character against the original.

3. Match the effort to the task. More reasoning helps with text and math. It helps little with images, so do not assume a longer "thinking" mode makes a screenshot read safe.

4. Keep a human on irreversible steps. Sending funds, signing transactions and changing settings should not rest on a single AI answer.

#5169. Bitcoin miners lose hashrate as hackers hijack up to 1,600 sites

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

On the 25th of November, Bitcoin mining company Braiins warned that attackers had hijacked Bitcoin miners’ work through unencrypted pool connections.

Machines kept running while someone else received credit. That basically left operators paying electricity bills for work credited elsewhere.

Its investigation documented four episodes on the 20th of November, mostly in Europe. Each affected 1,050–1,600 mining sites and diverted 0.6–1.9 EH/s for six to 49 minutes.

Attackers forged internet routing announcements, known as BGP hijacking, to intercept connections and impersonate the pool. Miners reconnected to the same address, making the switch difficult to spot.

Earlier episodes hit Latin America between the 7th and 12th of November.

Responding to an X user, Braiins said the attacks exploited a weakness in Stratum V1, the protocol connecting miners to pools. Stratum V2 contributor Pavlenex added,

This is an attack on MINERS and their infrastructure and is not a vulnerability in Braiins Pool.

The exposed protocol dates back to 2012, and warnings have been issued for years.

Braiins had flagged hashrate theft on the 18th of April 2020. It argued that preventing stolen revenue and reducing operating expenses would encourage upgrades more effectively than decentralization alone.

That history prompted Turtlecute, who works in product marketing at Braiins, to write,

When an X user asked whether this was the first publicly confirmed case, Pavlenex recalled earlier reports of interception attacks.

By November, the financial incentive for upgrading had become harder to dismiss. Braiins reported that miners’ machines showed normal activity while their pool dashboards recorded no credited hashrate.

Six months earlier, seven mining organizations had joined the Stratum V2 Working Group. These included ANTPOOL, Foundry, F2Pool, SpiderPool, Block, MARA Foundation, and DMND.

Reportedly, the organizations represented roughly 75% of the global hashrate at the time. Their backing gave the encrypted replacement substantial reach, but deployment remained uneven.

As of the 26th of November, the official directory listed Braiins Pool and DMND as production pools. It separately listed several solo pools and MARA Foundation’s industrial solo operation.

Foundry remained marked as work in progress, despite reported testing in November. ANTPOOL, F2Pool, and SpiderPool were absent from the production listings.

The exposure extended beyond V2 adoption. Braiins said most major pools’ public endpoints still offered only unencrypted Stratum V1 during its checks on the 23rd of November.

V2 encrypts mining traffic and verifies the pool’s identity, preventing an impersonator from receiving miners’ work. The November attacks showed the revenue consequences when industry support had yet to reach those connections.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) kept leaving crypto exchanges this week as the price of the meme cryptocurrency fell to levels last seen in the spring of 2021, and on Wednesday, the outflow picked up sharply.

According to CoinGlass data, 520.83 billion SHIB left exchanges over the past 24 hours. That amount made up most of the 757.51 billion SHIB that exchanges lost over the past seven days, and over the past 30 days, the outflow reached 2.88 trillion SHIB.

On Wednesday evening, SHIB was trading at $0.00000344, according to CoinGlass. So far this week, the token was down 4.78%, and its market capitalization went down to $2.02 billion, according to TradingView.

According to the weekly chart on TradingView, SHIB last traded at these levels in the spring of 2021, months before the token reached its all-time high of $0.00008845 on Oct. 28, 2021.

From early 2026 until mid-November, the price of SHIB held above $0.000004, and the yearly low stood at $0.00000411 at the July 17 close. In November, SHIB fell to $0.00000373, and in late November, the token dropped as low as $0.00000337. On Jan. 1, the token closed the day at $0.00000692, and since the start of the year, SHIB has lost 50.3% of its value, according to CoinGlass. As of Nov. 22, SHIB had lost 22.7% in November so far, according to CryptoRank.

The latest drop in SHIB came after Bitcoin fell back below $60,000 this week. On Saturday, Nov. 21, Bitcoin dropped as low as $55,150, its lowest price since September 2024. Over the past 24 hours, $57,590 worth of SHIB futures positions were liquidated, and $54,750 of that amount came from long positions on OKX, according to CoinGlass.

The Wednesday outflow was not the first large one this month. On Nov. 17, about 312 billion SHIB were withdrawn from exchanges, according to CryptoQuant. On the same day, the number of SHIB holders on Ethereum passed 1.7 million, according to Etherscan.

CoinGlass data also shows that since late 2024, the total SHIB balance on exchanges has gone down by 19.18 trillion tokens, or 20.54%, to 74.19 trillion, and over the same period, the price of SHIB fell by 88.39%. The remaining 74.19 trillion SHIB on exchanges make up 12.59% of the circulating supply and are worth about $254.75 million.

Most of the 24-hour outflow came from exchanges that CoinGlass groups as "Others," as their combined SHIB balance fell by 88.5% to 70.93 billion tokens. Over the same period, the SHIB balances of Binance and OKX barely changed, and Coinbase, Bitfinex and Bitstamp added SHIB.

As a result, in the week when the price of SHIB fell to levels last seen in 2021, exchanges lost more SHIB in a single day than over the previous six days combined, according to CoinGlass data.

Bitcoin posted a small bounce on Thursday, and the chart now hints at a move toward $66,000 next. US stock markets are shut for Thanksgiving, so trading volume could stay thin. In recent weeks, thin markets have produced some of Bitcoin’s wildest swings.

The bear market is not over yet, and no major low has been confirmed this year. The short-term picture has changed, though. For the first time since the decline began at the September high, there are signs that a local low may be in place. At every earlier stage of the sell-off, Bitcoin barely reacted and never tried to break resistance.

Selling pressure is also easing. Bitcoin is deeply oversold, negative momentum on the MACD is fading, and a bullish MACD crossover could appear soon. A similar setup in June did not mark the final bottom, but a local low did form there.

In the bearish case, Bitcoin’s rebound has already peaked as a weak three-leg bounce, and a new five-leg decline has started. The first leg down is done. A short relief bounce would come next, then a sharper third leg lower. That route points to roughly $40,000 or even lower.

In the bullish case, Bitcoin stays in a broad range and the current bounce runs further than expected. Recovery moves like this are often messy and hard to read. If it extends, Bitcoin could climb toward a long-term trendline around $90,000 or higher.

The key decision zone sits between $66,000 and $79,358. How Bitcoin trades there will likely decide which path plays out.

From the November low, Bitcoin first rose in three legs, helped partly by a rally in Nvidia. It made a higher high and broke above about $62,100, then slipped back into its range in another three-leg move.

The latest climb looks stronger. It now resembles a clean five-leg advance with no sign of a top yet, much like the recent move in S&P 500 futures. If that holds, a short pullback could come over the next few sessions before the next push higher. A move like that could also give altcoins a short-term lift.

Not yet. Even the most bullish near-term path points to around $90,000, and that would still count as a bounce inside a bear market. Before a run toward $100,000 can come into view, Bitcoin first needs to hold a higher low, break $62,100 and then clear the $66,000 to $79,358 zone. There is no clear timeline for that. The next few sessions will show whether the bounce has real strength.

We checked the numbers, and he is right about the coins, but the same test applied to Bitmine’s own shares tells a different story.

Lee’s numbers make a case for ETH as a coin that holds its value. But Bitmine shareholders do not own ETH directly. They own a slice of a company that keeps issuing new shares to buy more of it, and each new share dilutes that slice.

So does the hard-money case for ETH still hold for the people who own Bitmine stock, or is their share of Bitmine’s ETH being watered down faster than ETH’s supply grows?

Lee compared ETH with other big coins in Bitmine’s weekly update. Solana’s supply has grown 7.6% a year over the same period, XRP’s 5.4% and Cardano’s 2.9%, he said. “These others have been far more inflationary.”

Our own check, using CoinGecko’s daily circulating supply over the past 12 months, comes out almost the same:

Ethereum’s supply did grow about as slowly as Bitcoin’s over the past year. Most new ETH paid to validators is offset by the fees the network burns.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Reveals Upcoming Binance Listings

Bitmine paid for its ETH by printing shares. It had 232.4 million shares outstanding on August 31, 2025, and 613.3 million a year later, its annual report shows. By November 4, the count reached 626.5 million.

That is a 164% increase in one fiscal year, about 200 times ETH’s supply growth. Bitmine sold 395 million new shares through its at-the-market program in the Year to August, raising $12.9 billion.

Selling shares to buy ETH works for existing holders when the stock trades above the value of the coins behind it. It hurts when it trades below.

Right now, it trades below. Bitmine says its crypto, cash, and stakes are worth $11.1 billion, about $17.70 per share. At Monday’s close of $14.42, the market values Bitmine stock at roughly 0.81 times its assets, our estimate shows.

Bitmine has pushed back by buying its own shares. It repurchased 20.8 million shares at an average of $17 in July and August, and it has $3.6 billion left under its buyback plan.

EXPLORE: Ethereum News: BitMine To Halt Buying at 5% ETH Supply Cap

Bitmine now holds 6,085,564 ETH, or 4.98% of the 122.2 million in existence. Its stated goal is 5%, roughly 6.11 million ETH.

That leaves about 24,400 ETH to buy. At last week’s pace of 7,819 ETH, Bitmine would reach its target in about three weeks.

What happens after that matters for Bitmine stock. The weekly purchases have steadily driven demand for ETH, and Bitmine has said it would stop buying at 5%. With the stock below the value of its holdings, buybacks may use new money better than buying more ETH.

Most of the coins are already working. Bitmine stakes about 5.23 million ETH, 86% of its holdings, which it says earns about $245 million a year at current prices.

ETH trades at $1,698, below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $2,113, and its 200-day EMA at $2,242.

Lee has made a fair case that ETH is as scarce as Bitcoin. For Bitmine stock, though, the share count matters as much as the coin count, and that has grown far faster.

#5163. U.S. moves Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill forward with a 20-year lockup plan

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

The U.S. House Financial Services Committee has advanced H.R. 8957, known as the American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026, bringing the proposed legislation one step closer to a full House vote.

Introduced on the 21st of May 2026 by Republican Representative Nick Begich of Alaska, alongside Democratic Representative Jared Golden, the bill seeks to give the U.S. government’s Strategic Bitcoin [BTC] Reserve a formal legal foundation.

It proposes that the U.S. Treasury Department establish two separate structures within 180 days of the legislation becoming law. This includes a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve exclusively for Bitcoin and a Digital Asset Stockpile for other cryptocurrencies held by the federal government.

Under the proposal, Bitcoin owned by the federal government through criminal or civil asset forfeitures and other qualifying sources would be transferred to the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve.

Here, the most significant provision is a 20-year minimum holding requirement, which would prevent the government from selling, swapping, auctioning, or using reserve Bitcoin as collateral during that period. At the same time, the bill also allows the Treasury Department to explore budget-neutral ways of acquiring additional Bitcoin without increasing the national debt.

Separately, the legislation proposes a Digital Asset Stockpile to manage other cryptocurrencies held by the federal government. Lastly, it also introduces requirements for transparency, auditing, and congressional reporting to ensure proper oversight of these assets.

The bill is particularly significant because it seeks to give the U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve a statutory foundation. For its part, President Donald Trump had already established the reserve through an executive order in March 2025.

However, H.R. 8957 aims to formalize its structure and introduce additional safeguards, including the proposed 20-year holding period.

As of now, twenty months have already passed, and the U.S. government reportedly holds around 328,000 BTC, largely from seizures and forfeitures, while governments globally hold about 435,000 BTC.

Henceforth, if H.R. 8957 becomes law, the reserve would receive statutory backing, making it more difficult for a future administration to reverse the policy unilaterally.

The bill received approval from the House Financial Services Committee on 16th September 2026 in a 28-21 vote, with all Republican members voting in favor and all Democratic members opposing it.

Then, on the 24th of November, the committee formally reported the revised legislation to the full House, placing it on the Union Calendar and making it eligible for a floor vote. However, its chances of becoming law remain uncertain.

This is because the 119th Congress ends on the 3rd of January 2027, leaving limited time for the bill to pass the House, clear the Senate, and receive presidential approval.

Adding to this, market expectations also remain pessimistic, with Polymarket traders assigning only a 4% probability to the U.S. establishing a national Bitcoin reserve through legislation before 2027.

All of this coincided with Bitcoin trading at $60,355.92 at press time after a hike of 2.1% in the past 24 hours.

#5159. Bitcoin ‘As Important as It’s Ever Been’ if Inflation Rises, Coinbase CEO Says

"Bitcoin investors tend to sell BTC when there's a big IPO. Then they come back."

That's Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong's take on Bitcoin investor behavior, less than a week after the record-breaking $93.5 billion IPO of Claude creator Anthropic.

"Historically, people rotate out of it to take advantage of a big IPO. Then they come back in," Armstrong wrote on X earlier today.

The limited window of opportunity to invest in an IPO helps explain the behavior Armstrong described. For an investor to buy at the IPO price, there's only a certain period during which they can request an allocation of shares. After that, the price is determined by the market.

On Nov. 19, Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq, and that brief window of opportunity mattered.

Shares were priced at $83, up from the $70-$78 range indicated just two days earlier. Anthropic's stock, trading under the ticker ANT, opened at $111.50.

If you bought at that opening price, you paid about 34% more per share than an investor who received an allocation at the IPO price.

When the IPO closed on Nov. 20, 1.127 billion shares had been sold, including 147 million additional shares purchased by underwriters exercising their option.

Of the $93.5 billion in gross proceeds, Anthropic itself received around $91.6 billion. The rest went to existing shareholders.

There was also a separate $26 billion private placement involving investors such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Google and others. In total, the combined transactions were valued at $119.5 billion.

As for the longer-term case for holding BTC, Armstrong's point concerns investors' expectations about the future purchasing power of their money.

"If you think there is going to be more inflation and money printing in the future, bitcoin is as important as ever."

At the heart of the matter is Bitcoin's 21 million supply limit.

If you expect governments to continue expanding the money supply, you may still be excited by the prospect of a major IPO. And you may sell some of your BTC to participate in it.

Armstrong's argument is that the window of opportunity to participate in a major IPO eventually closes.

However, the reasons investors bought Bitcoin in the first place may remain long after the newly listed stock starts trading.

Bitcoin wallets could be linked to user IP addresses with 100% accuracy and for just about $0.34.

The flaw relies on the network's automatic rebroadcasting of small transactions that may have been out on hold by miners prioritizing higher fee transfers.

This is another in a recent line of Bitcoin vulnerabilities, including a hashrate hijacking spree and rumours of AI breaking ECC encryption.

According to Bitcoin Core contributor Abubakar Sadiq Ismail, the intrusion begins when an attacker sends low-fee ‘dust’ tokens to a BTC address.

Since miners prioritize higher-fee transactions, sending low amounts naturally takes longer time frames. The Bitcoin Core software automatically broadcasts stuck transactions after 12-36 hours, at which point an attacker is able to see the receiver’s IP address.

The method achieved a 100% success rate across 30 simulations on a regression test (regtest) network for only 18-34 cents per attempt.

At present, the flaw remains unpatched, and attackers are still able to get the exact location of Bitcoin wallets, in addition to viewing their balances.

And while no funds are at risk, such information could be used in crypto wrench attacks where an individual is physically targeted in a cryptocurrency robbery.

For now, Bitcoiners can choose manual wallet broadcasting in place of automatic broadcasts.

CoinPedia recently covered how attackers are hijacking Bitcoin hashrate, directing mining proceeds to their own wallets.

Even more, rumours still abound of OpenAI and Anthropic breaking several cryptographic security methods, including Elliptic Curve Cryptography, which Bitcoin relies upon.

The price of BTC remains unaffected by these reports, trading at around $60,000 for the last couple of days.

#5155. JPMorgan, HSBC and StoneX Trade Digital Gold in London as Tokenized Gold Holdings Jump 48%

London is testing tokenized gold as Tether Gold and PAX Gold holdings climb 48% to $4.6 billion despite falling gold prices.

JPMorgan, HSBC and StoneX completed the first live wholesale trades of fractional tokenized gold in London last week. The test is meant to keep the world’s largest gold market ahead of Asian rivals. The three firms also used the digital gold as collateral, without moving a single bar out of the vaults.

Bloomberg reported the trades on Tuesday. They ran on a system built by the World Gold Council (WGC), the industry body that led the project. David Tait, the WGC’s chief executive, called it “a historic step forward for the gold market.”

JPMORGAN $JPM, HSBC AND STONEX COMPLETE THE FIRST LIVE WHOLESALE TRADES OF FRACTIONAL DIGITAL GOLD IN LONDON, ALSO USING IT AS COLLATERAL pic.twitter.com/bwVAdrpkXh

— The Wolf Of All Streets (@scottmelker) November 24, 2026

The banks did not say how much gold changed hands. The system is still in testing, and there is no date yet for a wider launch. The timing is awkward for gold itself. The metal trades near $3,626 an ounce, 32% below its January record and 11% lower than a year ago.

What changes for London’s bullion market, and does it matter for crypto’s own gold tokens?

The WGC calls the new format “pooled gold interests.” Each one is a fractional, electronically transferable share in a pool of physical bars held in approved London vaults.

That fills a gap. Most London trades today are in unallocated gold, which is cheap to hold but leaves buyers as creditors if their bank fails. Allocated gold means owning specific bars, which is safer but costly and hard to split. The WGC proposed the pooled model with law firm Linklaters in September 2025 as a third route between the two.

The collateral piece matters most. Banks could pledge gold for loans and margin as easily as they post bonds, without trucks or vault transfers.

London has a lot riding on it. Its over-the-counter market handles more than $180 billion of gold trades a day, and its vaults held $1.4 trillion of gold in August. Hong Kong, working with the Shanghai Gold Exchange, began testing its own gold clearing system in July.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Predicts Best Low-Cap Crypto

The London pilot is a closed, bank-only system. Crypto has run its own version for years with Tether Gold (XAUT) and PAX Gold (PAXG), and those tokens have been growing fast.

We read the supply of both tokens straight from their Ethereum contracts, where each token equals one troy ounce. We compared that with CoinGecko’s figures from a year ago.

So crypto’s digital gold kept adding ounces even as the gold price fell. Still, the two tokens hold about 0.33% of the value of gold sitting in London’s vaults. The whole tokenized gold category traded about $329 million in the past 24 hours on CoinGecko, against London’s $180 billion a day.

Explore: RLUSD Surpasses Trump’s USD1 Stablecoin but XRP Still Sinks 26%

PAX Gold tracks the metal closely. On Binance, PAXG trades at $3,637, below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $3,945, and its 200-day EMA at $4,195.

Last week’s sell-off pushed it to $3,491 on Saturday, its lowest level in 300 days. Sellers led on Binance’s spot market, where the token itself changes hands. Orders that sold at the market price right away outweighed buyers by a net $13.4 million over the past seven days.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Reveals Upcoming Coinbase Listings

The WGC still has to settle governance rules and a launch date. If the big banks adopt digital gold for collateral, the gap between London’s vaults and crypto’s gold tokens could start to close.
